title: The sage who knew only the words
hookLine: Narada has studied everything, and admits he knows only the words
carry: ritambhara: knowing it, not knowing about it
last: THE CLEAR MIND TAKES THE COLOR.

cards: Narada is the sage who has studied everything. In the Chandogya Upanishad he comes to another sage, Sanatkumara, and asks to be taught. Sanatkumara says: first tell me what you already know.
So Narada lists it. The four Vedas. The old histories and stories.
Grammar, mathematics, logic, the rites for the ancestors, the lore of the stars and of the gods, the fine arts. It's a long list. Then he says the line the whole chapter hangs on.

teach.b: Sir, I know only the words. I don't know the self. I've heard from people like you that whoever knows the self crosses beyond sorrow, and I am in sorrow.
Take me across. Sanatkumara's reply is gentle and blunt: all you've studied is only name. Then he leads him, step by step, toward what the Upanishad calls fullness.
That's a real Hindu teaching, and it runs deep: knowing about the sacred isn't the same as knowing it. Narada's learning isn't mocked. It's the start, not the end.
Patanjali gives that difference a name. Sutra 1.47: when the subtle absorption without reflection becomes fully clear, there's inner serenity, adhyatma prasada.
Sutra 1.48: there, wisdom is ritambhara, truth-bearing. Ritam echoes rita, the old Vedic word for the cosmic order, the rightness that turns the seasons, tied to truth itself.
So ritambhara is wisdom that carries the truth in it, because the mind adds no color of its own. Sutra 1.49 says how it differs.

What you learn from testimony, a teacher or a book, and from inference, reasoning it out, is about things in general. Truth-bearing wisdom knows the particular, as it is. Narada knew all the words, and not the self.
Then sutra 1.50: every experience leaves an impression, a samskara, a groove in the mind.

teach.h: A GROOVE THAT BLOCKS THE OTHERS.
teach.b: This wisdom leaves a groove so deep it blocks the old ruts. One groove is left, its own. Tomorrow, what happens when even that goes quiet.

how: Hindu teachers honor scripture study but often say it must ripen into direct knowing; in classical yoga, ritambhara prajna is described as the fruit of mature absorption, set apart from book learning and reasoning, both valued as steps on the way.

o: a clever argument that proves what's true
knowing a thing as it is, with nothing added
knowledge gathered from many good books

games.q: words and knowing: tap the pairs.
p: an impression, a groove in the mind

s: Narada came to Sanatkumara knowing very little
he listed the Vedas, histories, grammar, mathematics and more, and still said he knew only words.
Patanjali says truth-bearing wisdom is just better reasoning
1.49: testimony and inference know things in general; this wisdom knows the particular.
rita is a Vedic word for the cosmic order
the rightness that turns the seasons, tied to truth.

games.q: you've read every book about the ocean, but never seen it. then you stand on the shore. which kind of knowledge is closer to ritambhara?
o: the shore: knowing this ocean, directly.
games.why: 1.49: testimony and inference know things in general. truth-bearing wisdom knows the particular, as it is.

practice: In many Hindu homes a small bell rings at puja. Ring one if you have it, or tap a glass, or listen to whatever sound is near. Notice the word bell arrive, and the ideas about it.
Let them go and stay with the sound itself, this sound, as it fades. When it's gone, rest in the quiet it leaves, then begin again.

wordCard.voice: Truth-bearing wisdom. Ritambhara prajna, sutra 1.48: the knowing that arises in the clearest absorption, full of truth, and aimed at the particular, as it is.

orig.note: Sanskrit ṛtambharā: truth-bearing, full of rita, the Vedic word for cosmic order and truth.

carryVoice: Your line: ritambhara, knowing it, not knowing about it. Narada's whole library, and still: take me across. That's day four hundred forty-five.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 7.1.1–3 (Narada lists his learning; 'I know only the words, not the self'; all this is only name)
Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.47–1.50 (inner serenity; ritambhara prajna; its object; its impression)
Rig Veda (rita as cosmic order, e.g. hymns to Varuna and Mitra)
